title: Painting the Walls
statement:
There are `n` walls to paint, described by two arrays of length `n`: `cost` and `time`. Two painters share the job:

- The **paid** painter can take wall `i`; it then spends `time[i]` time units on it and charges `cost[i]`.
- The **free** painter can take any wall, spends exactly 1 time unit on it and charges nothing, but it may only work during time units in which the paid painter is busy with a wall.

Every wall must be painted by one of the two painters. Return the smallest total amount of money that gets all `n` walls painted.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every set of paid walls works but costs O(2^n). Look at one paid wall instead: while the paid painter spends `time[i]` units on wall `i`, the free painter can finish `time[i]` other walls. So paying `cost[i]` takes care of `time[i] + 1` walls in total. The question becomes a 0/1 knapsack: pick walls to pay for so that their "coverage" adds up to at least `n`, at the lowest cost. Coverage beyond `n` is useless, so it is capped at `n`.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[covered]` be the cheapest cost found so far that takes care of at least `covered` walls. Start with `dp[0] = 0` and everything else `Infinity`.
2. For each wall `i`, try paying for it. Walk `covered` from `n` down to 1 so each wall is used at most once.
3. Paying for wall `i` covers `time[i] + 1` walls, so the rest needs `before = max(0, covered - time[i] - 1)` walls covered.
4. Keep the cheaper of the old `dp[covered]` and `dp[before] + cost[i]`.
5. Return `dp[n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`cost = [1,2,3,2]`, `time = [1,2,3,2]`, `n = 4`, `dp = [0,∞,∞,∞,∞]`.

- Wall 0 covers 2 walls for 1: `dp = [0,1,1,∞,∞]`.
- Wall 1 covers 3 walls for 2: `dp[3] = dp[0] + 2 = 2`, `dp[4] = dp[1] + 2 = 3`, so `dp = [0,1,1,2,3]`.
- Wall 2 covers 4 walls for 3 and wall 3 covers 3 walls for 2; neither beats the current values.

The answer is `dp[4] = 3`: pay for walls 0 and 1.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each of the `n` walls updates `n` states.
- Space: O(n) for the `dp` row.

## Pitfalls

- A paid wall counts itself too: it covers `time[i] + 1` walls, not `time[i]`.
- Loop `covered` downwards; going upwards lets one wall be paid for twice.
- Clamp `before` at 0 instead of indexing a negative position; covering more walls than needed is fine.
- Greedy by cost or by `cost / time` ratio fails; the coverage has to be combined exactly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of walls |
| `dp[covered]` | cheapest cost that takes care of at least `covered` walls |
| `i` | the wall being considered for the paid painter |
| `covered` | the coverage target being updated |
| `before` | coverage still needed from earlier walls if wall `i` is paid for |

narration.2: Count the walls; that is the coverage the answer needs.
narration.3: dp[covered] will hold the cheapest cost that takes care of at least covered walls; nothing is reachable yet.
narration.6: Consider each wall once as a candidate for the paid painter.
narration.7: Go through coverage targets from high to low so this wall is not used twice.
narration.8: Paying for wall i covers time[i] + 1 walls, so this is how many earlier walls still need covering (at least 0).
narration.9: Keep the cheaper of skipping wall i or paying for it on top of dp[before].
narration.12: dp[n] is the cheapest way to get every wall painted.
